tip: Retrieval-augmented generation: a language model first looks up relevant documents, then writes its answer using what it found.
A search that combines keyword matching with meaning-based vector search, so results can match either the exact words or the idea.
A simple way to merge several ranked result lists into one, giving each item more credit the higher it ranks in each list.
An open model from the Allen Institute for AI that turns scientific papers into numeric vectors so similar papers can be found.
A model that reads a query and a document together and scores how relevant they are, more accurate but slower than comparing precomputed vectors.
A second pass over search results that reorders a shortlist with a slower, more careful model so the best matches come first.
An open-source database that stores data alongside vector embeddings and supports both keyword and similarity search over them.
A web standard that lets a server push updates to a browser over one open connection, so results appear as they are ready.
Low-rank adaptation: a way to fine-tune a large model by training a small set of added weights instead of changing all of them.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: methods that adapt a large pretrained model by training only a small fraction of its parameters.
Storing a model's numbers at lower precision, such as 4 bits instead of 16, so it uses less memory and runs on modest hardware.
A method that fits a curve that never goes down, often used to turn raw model scores into probabilities that match real outcomes.
Deciding whether two records, such as two product listings or two customer entries, describe the same real-world thing.
Using a large language model to grade or rank answers or search results, as a faster and cheaper stand-in for human reviewers.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain: a ranking score from 0 to 1 that rewards putting the most relevant results near the top.
A statistic from minus 1 to 1 that measures how closely two rankings agree, counting pairs of items placed in the same order.
Matthews correlation coefficient: a score from minus 1 to 1 for yes or no predictions that stays reliable when one outcome is rare.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, used in credit scoring to measure how well a model's scores separate good accounts from bad ones.
An open-source library for gradient-boosted decision trees, widely used as a strong baseline for predictions from tables of data.
Open-source software that schedules jobs on shared computing clusters, queuing each job until the GPUs or CPUs it asks for are free.
A standard encryption method, approved by NIST, that keeps data secret and also detects whether anyone has tampered with it.
A Google Cloud service that runs an app packaged as a container and scales it with traffic, with no servers to manage.
A Docker setting that links a folder on the host computer into a container, so both see and change the same files.
An entity matching method from 2020 research that fine-tunes a pretrained language model such as BERT to decide whether two records match.
An extra penalty added during training that pushes a model to perform about equally well across different groups of data.
An image model that learns to turn noise into a clean picture step by step, built on a U-shaped network that keeps fine detail.
A model that learns to translate images from one style or domain to another without needing matched before and after pairs.
A score from 0 to 1 for how much a predicted region, such as a tumor outline, overlaps the true one.
An algorithm that generates maps or patterns by filling a grid one tile at a time so each tile fits its neighbors.
A way to score how important a word is to one document, higher when it is common there but rare across the others.
Latent Dirichlet allocation: a statistical model that discovers topics in a set of documents by finding words that tend to appear together.
